catalog_locator: Ch. 5 Tones: sec. 5.1 Lexical Tone, p. 63; end of sec. 5.1.4 and sec. 5.2 Grammatical Tone, pp. 73-74
catalog_quote: Tsuvaɗi exhibits two level tones in its lexicon: High (H), Low (L), and one contour High-Low, or High-Falling (HL). All three can be observed in nouns with the noun class prefix hAC-, which consistently bears high tone: ... Phonetically, the Low tone can be realized as a level or—more frequently at the end of words—a low falling pitch. However, the falling pitch starting at Low tone is considered an allotone (phonetic variant) of Low. For example, items (e), (f) and (g) are considered to have the same tones by native speakers. Since most words were elicited in isolation, the perception of falling pitch is likely due to the word-final transition to the following pause or silence. ... Automatic downdrifting also occurs word-internally, as observed in examples (b), (c) and (d). [p. 63] ... Verbs in the Realis, Irrealis, and Imperative do not appear to have lexically assigned tone, but instead show grammatical tone. (cf. Section 5.2 on Grammatical Tone). ... In Tsuvaɗi, all verbs exhibit grammatical tone and are lexically toneless. For disyllabic verb roots in the Realis mood, the verb takes a L-H.L melody on the index and root. In the Irrealis mood, the [p. 73] verb takes a H-L.HL melody on the index and root. [p. 74]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tsuvaɗi is described as a tone language with two level tones (H, L) and an HL contour on nouns, automatic downdrift, and grammatical (mood-driven) tone melodies on lexically toneless verbs. Neither Buttacavoli 2022 nor Blench 2007 (sec. 3.3 Tones, p. 5: 'high, low and falling') mentions stress, accent or prominence at all, so no word-stress position can be assigned; the language is tonal per both sources and silent on stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress (none discussed). Tone: HL on the noun-class prefix is rare (p. 70); word-final L takes a falling allotone in isolation (p. 63).
new_statements.domain_note: Words elicited in isolation from a ~2000-item recorded wordlist (citation forms); nouns = class prefix + root, 2-4 syllables (p. 53). No phrase-level prosody beyond downdrift in associative constructions (p. 72).
new_statements.identity_note: Buttacavoli 2022 describes the Tsudugu (Adugu) dialect, the Bible-translation target lect (data from Momo, Azhezhaha, Udara, Tudun Muntsira, Idaci villages); Glottolog gives Tsudugu no separate glottocode (its record reads 'Tsugudu = Tsuvadi [tvd]'), and the SIL survey's two named dialects are Tsuvaɗi-Agaɗi (Azagaɗi, east) and Tsuvaɗi-Azozolo (west). Blench 2007 is based on a 1999 session at Ragara plus David Lovelace's 1990 lexical data (dialect unspecified). Both fall under tsuv1239; no dialect-level glottocode exists.
